name: Tatarstan
summary_text: Tatarstan stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that includes anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation.  Same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are prohibited, trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since 2023, and no discrimination protection exists. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records at least 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.  Human Rights Watch reported 101 extremism-related convictions by 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or display of its symbols, comprising 98 administrative and 3 criminal cases. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation, two sentenced to prison and seventeen pending or unknown.  On 15 May 2025, three staff of two publishing houses were charged with running an extremist organisation under article 282.2 and face up to 12 years in prison. Repeated display of banned symbols is punishable by up to four years in prison.  The UK Home Office note places the elevated state-persecution exception, which covers trans people, public LGBT+ advocates and North Caucasus residents likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, outside ordinary regions such as Tatarstan.

name: Tuva
summary_text: The Republic of Tyva (Tuva) stands under the national framework of Russia, and the source inventory contains no division-specific transgender evidence for this republic. A trans visitor to Tuva is therefore assessed against the countrywide regime as it operates there.  Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the position has hardened since 2022. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and legal gender recognition are banned: the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and gender changes on official documents was signed in 2023, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. The Supreme Court of Russia designated the international LGBT+ movement an extremist organisation in November 2023. The expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that includes, explicitly, anything justifying gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and the US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers.  The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) is the framework this republic is assessed against. It records that between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement, that 'gay propaganda' fines for individuals reach 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention, and that the note carries no information specific to Tuva beyond the national framework. The same Home Office policy affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the standard for UK asylum claims.  Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the designated International LGBT Movement or for displaying its symbols since the November 2023 ruling, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. It also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. That article carries no Tuva-specific detail; it sets the national enforcement baseline against which Tuva is scored, and Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.  Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding June 2025. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.  Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. In July 2024 the BBC followed a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.
